summary:
Throughout history, humanity has looked to the sky in search of what lies beyond our world. Today, the volume of astronomical data far exceeds what individual researchers can analyze alone. For the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we developed AstroForge, a web application that bridges the gap between the general public and data from SPHEREx, NASA’s all-sky spectral survey mission, enabling anyone to explore the universe and contribute to new discoveries.

By harnessing a distributed network of observers, AstroForge broadens public engagement and accelerates scientific progress. Users can select moving objects directly on the displayed images and mark the same object across multiple observations to reconstruct its relative position to the Sun and can examine the distribution and density of molecules across the observed image. When a finding is saved, its file stores every recorded value together with the resulting trajectory, so it can be reopened and continued in a later observation. This dedicated filing and archiving system also supports asynchronous review. To help users interpret their results, the platform provides specialized classification algorithms and an interactive spectrum viewer designed specifically for SPHEREx data.
details:
Project Overview

AstroForge is a Python-based web application that makes NASA’s SPHEREx data accessible to everyone. It lets anyone explore, document and analyze astronomical observations, then turns those observations into archived, reusable scientific records.

1. What does it do and how does it work?

AstroForge is built in Python. Incoming data is retrieved with Astropy and Astroquery, and we deliberately prioritize NASA’s primary data sources so that every observation rests on authoritative, reliable information.

The platform has one core observation module and two additional modules:

Observation module (core): Users enter the values they want in a natural, intuitive way and explore SPHEREx data with ease. Every observation can be filed and archived, which makes it simple to find within very large datasets and straightforward to reuse in scientific research.

Spectral analysis module: This module analyzes light across different wavelengths to study how light is distributed and to enable the detection of molecular absorption features in the observed object.

Relative position module: Users mark a moving object across a short video of six consecutive SPHEREx images. From the marked points, the platform calculates the object’s position relative to the Sun and displays it as a three-dimensional visualization. The results are recorded in the same archive, so they can be reopened and continued in later observations.

Molecular Spectral Mapping and Analysis Module:Molecular Spectral Mapping and Analysis combines HITRAN molecular line data with SPHEREx FITS observations, calculating theoretical absorption spectra (Voigt profiles, optical depth, transmittance) and mapping molecular transition strengths onto each pixel’s wavelength range to produce color-coded molecular overlays on the astronomical image.

2. What benefits does it have?

Accessibility: Users do not need specialist knowledge or software to begin exploring SPHEREx data. They simply enter the values they are interested in, and the platform handles data retrieval and processing in the background.

Organized discovery: The filing and archiving system stores every observation together with its recorded values, so findings remain easy to locate even within very large datasets instead of getting lost.

Scientific usability: Archived records are structured so they can be reused directly in scientific research, and they support asynchronous review, allowing observations to be checked and continued by others at a later time.

Depth beyond observation: Rather than only marking a point in the sky, AstroForge helps users understand what an object is. Spectral analysis reveals molecular absorption features, and orbit tracking reveals how the object moves over the years.

Reliable foundations: Because data is drawn primarily from NASA’s own sources, users can trust the information they build their observations on.

Continuity: Saved observations and orbits can be reopened in later sessions, so exploration is never a one-time activity but an ongoing process.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

Our primary goal is to bring astronomical discoveries to the general public and to spark lasting interest in the sky and in science. Many people are curious about space but never get the chance to work with real data, because the tools are either too complex or simply out of reach. AstroForge is designed to change that by giving everyone a simple yet meaningful way to take part in real observation.

Beyond public engagement, the project aims to make a scientific contribution. The volume of astronomical data now available is far larger than individual researchers can analyze alone. By enabling a distributed network of observers, each documenting and archiving their findings in a consistent, reusable format, AstroForge helps share this workload and turns public curiosity into usable scientific records.

In the long term, we hope the platform inspires a new generation of observers who not only look at the sky but also understand what they see, and who feel they are part of the ongoing story of astronomical discovery.

4. What tools, languages, hardware or software did you use?

Languages: Python, JavaScript, HTML, CSS

Main libraries: Astropy, Astroquery, NumPy, Matplotlib, HAPI, pathlib, truststore, json, os, csv, threading, queue, concurrent.futures

Data source: NASA’s primary SPHEREx data archives

Platform: Web application

5. How is your project creative?

Most tools let people simply look at a point of light. AstroForge goes further by revealing what that point actually is: its density, its characteristics and its motion over time. We also wanted to bring a genuine astronomical feeling to the experience, so users feel like observers rather than spectators.

Molecular Spectral Mapping and Analysis

This feature connects molecular spectroscopy with infrared astronomical observations by bringing HITRAN reference data and SPHEREx measurements into a shared analytical framework. It retrieves molecular transition parameters, including line positions and intensities, and calculates theoretical absorption spectra using Voigt line profiles under specified temperature and pressure conditions. By incorporating column density, the model also derives optical depth and transmittance across the selected wavelength range.

Beyond theoretical modeling, the feature processes SPHEREx FITS observations using their associated spectral calibration products and WCS information. It generates pixel-level wavelength and bandwidth maps, allowing the wavelength range associated with each detector pixel to be identified. HITRAN molecular transition strengths are associated with the corresponding pixel-level wavelength intervals, producing molecular transition correspondence maps and combined, color-coded visualizations over the astronomical image.

Relative Position

The relative position module is where this idea becomes most tangible. Users are shown a short video made of six consecutive SPHEREx images and can click on the moving object in each frame. Every click is recorded and layered on top of the previous ones, so the object’s position builds up across the sequence. From these marked points, AstroForge performs the necessary calculations to determine the object’s position relative to the Sun and draws the result as an interactive three-dimensional visualization. What begins as a few clicks on flat images becomes a spatial model that users can view from different angles.

6. What factors did your team consider?

The most important factor was ease of use. We wanted a platform simple enough for anyone to pick up, yet capable of supporting comprehensive research. Alongside that, we prioritized reliable data sourcing from NASA’s primary archives, and a filing system that keeps findings organized and reusable.
